methodology.payload_basis: Maximum advertised payload to a reference Low Earth Orbit, expendable configuration where a vehicle can fly both expendable and reusable. This is the standard basis used in public $/kg comparisons (e.g. CSIS Aerospace Security).

price_basis_values.dedicated_list: Published commercial list price for a dedicated launch. Most comparable across vehicles.
price_basis_values.rideshare: Published per-kilogram rideshare price. What a small customer actually pays.
price_basis_values.gov_contract: Reported government contract or program price. Includes mission assurance and infrastructure costs a commercial buyer would not pay.
price_basis_values.program_cost: Total program cost divided by flights flown. Includes development. Not comparable to a commercial list price.
price_basis_values.estimate: No published price. Analyst estimate or reported range.

caveats: List price is an upper bound on marginal cost and a lower bound on what a government buyer pays. The two are not the same number and should not be compared casually.
Reusable vehicles almost never fly at max expendable payload. Effective $/kg actually paid is higher than the figure shown here.
Prices are nominal USD in the stated price_year and are NOT inflation-adjusted. Comparing a 2008 figure to a 2026 figure without deflating overstates the decline.
price_basis is not constant across rows. Filter on it before computing any cross-sectional statistic.
confidence: high = published commercial price; medium = credible reporting or government audit; low = estimate, contested figure, or currency/basis mismatch.

vehicles.name: Falcon Heavy
vehicles.notes: Lowest list $/kg of any operational vehicle, but only at max fully-expendable payload, which no customer has ever actually bought. Treat as a theoretical floor.

vehicles.name: New Glenn
vehicles.source: Blue Origin has not published a list price. Reported estimates span $68-110M; the upper bound is used here as the conservative figure.
vehicles.notes: First flight 16 Jan 2025 (NG-1, reached orbit). First booster recovery on NG-3, 19 Apr 2026. A pad anomaly during a hotfire test at LC-36 on 28 May 2026 interrupted the flight campaign. Range is wide because no price is published; at the low end this vehicle would beat Falcon 9.

vehicles.name: Falcon 9 Block 5
vehicles.source: SpaceX published list price, $74M standard payment plan for 2026 (up from $70M in 2025, $69.75M in 2024, $67M in 2022, $62M in 2018)
vehicles.notes: Nominal list price has risen roughly 19% since 2018 even as the frontier narrative says launch is getting cheaper. Both are true: the frontier fell because Falcon Heavy and reuse arrived, not because Falcon 9's sticker price fell.

vehicles.name: Neutron
vehicles.source: Rocket Lab announced target price ~$50M per launch; vehicle has not flown
vehicles.notes: PROJECTED. Debut slipped repeatedly; as of Aug 2026 the window for a 2026 first flight was reported as narrowing. Excluded from active-vehicle statistics.

vehicles.name: Vulcan Centaur (VC6)
vehicles.notes: Price is the starting figure; actual price varies substantially with solid booster count. VC6 is the six-booster maximum configuration, so pairing the max payload with the starting price flatters this row.

vehicles.name: PSLV-XL
vehicles.source: Rs 130-200 crore, approx $16-24M (2023); ~$21M commonly cited for PSLV-XL
vehicles.notes: Workhorse for sun-synchronous and small missions. Low absolute price, modest payload. Domestic Indian cost structure is not directly comparable to Western commercial pricing.

vehicles.name: Ariane 6 (A64)
vehicles.source: EUR 115M per-launch estimate (2018), converted at 1.08 USD/EUR. Arianespace does not publish per-flight pricing.
vehicles.notes: Weakest row in the dataset and flagged as such. The underlying figure is a 2018 euro-denominated estimate for a vehicle that first flew in 2024, carried here in nominal converted dollars. Do not treat as a current price.

vehicles.name: Long March 5
vehicles.source: Estimated ~$160M per launch; Chinese pricing is not publicly listed
vehicles.notes: Not sold to Western customers, so there is no market-clearing price to observe. State-directed pricing makes the $/kg figure close to meaningless as an economic signal.

vehicles.name: Falcon 9 (Transporter rideshare)
vehicles.source: SpaceX Smallsat Rideshare Program published pricing, $350,000 for 50 kg to SSO, $7,000/kg beyond (Transporter-16 onward, 2026)
vehicles.notes: This is the single most useful row in the dataset and the one most often left out of $/kg charts. A small customer buying access today pays about 2.2x the Falcon 9 dedicated max-payload rate and 4.6x the Falcon Heavy rate. The frontier number is not the transacted number.

vehicles.name: Atlas V 551
vehicles.source: Reported cost per launch $110-153M (2016); upper bound used for the 551 configuration
vehicles.notes: Most powerful Atlas V variant, phased out for Vulcan. Government contract pricing includes mission assurance a commercial customer does not buy.

vehicles.name: Ariane 5 ECA
vehicles.notes: Dual-GTO workhorse. Retired in favour of Ariane 6, which on current estimates is not dramatically cheaper per kg.

vehicles.name: Saturn V
vehicles.source: Inflation-adjusted per-launch cost; ~$185M nominal 1969, variously adjusted to $1.0-1.5B depending on dollar-year and allocation of development cost
vehicles.notes: Highest payload ever flown. Published estimates range roughly $6,300-8,800/kg depending on dollar-year and payload assumption. Heavily contested; included for historical perspective only.

vehicles.name: Soyuz-2 (Soyuz-ST, Kourou)
vehicles.source: Arianespace commercial Soyuz-ST at Kourou ~$80M; domestic Roscosmos launches reported as low as ~$35M
vehicles.notes: Basis mismatch flagged: the price is the Kourou commercial figure while the payload is the standard Soyuz-2.1b LEO figure, so this row mixes two configurations. Western commercial availability ended in 2022; status reflects commercial availability, not Russian domestic flights, which continue.

vehicles.name: Delta IV Heavy
vehicles.source: Reported per-launch cost ~$350M; NRO missions reported at ~$440M
vehicles.notes: Most expensive Western vehicle per launch. Flew high-value national security payloads where schedule assurance dominated price.

vehicles.name: Space Shuttle
vehicles.source: Total program cost averaged over all missions, inflation-adjusted to 2008 USD, ~$1.5B per launch; total program spend ~$196B through 2011
vehicles.notes: Program-cost basis, which is why it towers over every other row. Marginal per-flight cost was far lower (~$450M). The honest comparison is program cost to program cost, and almost nobody makes it. Reusability pursued without cheap refurbishment.

vehicles.name: Starship
vehicles.source: Began deploying operational payloads in 2026; no published commercial price
vehicles.notes: NO PRICE. Stated targets range from $100-200/kg (Musk, May 2026) to internal per-launch cost estimates around $25M, but none of these is a price a customer can buy at. Deliberately excluded from every $/kg statistic in this repository. Including aspirational targets in cost curves is the most common error in launch-cost analysis.
